clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 70s with HLA-B51 homozygosity and long-standing ocular involvement (uveitis and retinitis pigmentosa since his 30s, resulting in blindness) presented with acute neurological symptoms: gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria, and dysphagia over three days. MRI revealed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus with DWI/ADC hyperintensity, no gadolinium enhancement, and MR spectroscopy showing neuroinflammation pattern (elevated choline, preserved NAA). On admission, physical examination showed no skin rash, vulvar ulcers, stomatitis, and pathergy test was negative. CSF analysis was normal without pleocytosis or elevated IL-6, and oligoclonal IgG bands were negative. Blood work showed normal WBC and negative autoimmune antibodies (RF, ANA, ANCA, AQP4, MOG). Based on acute brainstem lesion, MRI findings, and HLA-B51 positivity, the patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral corticosteroid and colchicine. His symptoms gradually ameliorated, and at 2 months follow-up, he returned home with minor sequelae of mild left hemiparesis and gait disturbance.
